# Deciding what goes in the index?

Day 2, 15:40 · Google · coverage: transcript

Same speaker and recording as Calculating (some) signals.

## Claims

- **[Stage]** Google's index is immense but finite, so Google cannot index every URL it finds on a web with a practically infinite number of URLs.
  > "our index is immense. Like, immense. But it is a finite resource."
  <br><sub>`D2-C680` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Repeats [D1-C037](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Repeats [D2-C344](../day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) · Repeated by [D3-C256](../day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google gives two reasons for not indexing every URL it knows: most of them would not be useful to users, and including URLs in the index that users would never see would be an immense investment.
  <br><sub>`D2-C681` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's index selection system calculates thresholds and decides which documents are kept and which are thrown out; a URL that does not meet the thresholds is not indexed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C682` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extends [D1-C211](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Index selection*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection aims to index only documents that are useful to users now or potentially in the future.
  <br><sub>`D2-C683` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection is a predictive AI system that relies heavily on machine learning.
  <br><sub>`D2-C684` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C037](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection uses what Google already knows about a site: if the site, or even a section of it, satisfies users' needs well, new URLs from it are treated more forgivingly.
  > "the index selection system is going to be more forgiving when it sees a new URL from your site"
  <br><sub>`D2-C685` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C094](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-10`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Launch new pages under sections that Google already indexes well, and improve or remove weak sections, because index selection judges new URLs partly by what it knows about the site and the section they sit in.
  <br><sub>`D2-C686` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · Extends [D1-C095](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection uses the signals calculated earlier in indexing for each document it has to select or discard.
  <br><sub>`D2-C687` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C205](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Index selection*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C688` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C026](../day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extends [D1-C211](../day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Index selection*</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google's coverage of a country is limited, index selection becomes more likely to select documents relevant to that country, even if other signals would suggest otherwise.
  <br><sub>`D2-C689` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google lacks content in a language, such as Basque, index selection becomes more likely to select lower-quality documents in that language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C690` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Under-served languages were presented as an opportunity: where Google's index holds a lot of spam in a language such as Basque, a site that starts publishing in that language can very likely replace that spam with its own content and rank for those keywords (one clause of the reasoning was inaudible).
  <br><sub>`D2-C691` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.
  <br><sub>`D2-C692` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The overall importance of a document or site plays a significant role in index selection.
  <br><sub>`D2-C693` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** News sites were given as the example of importance at work in index selection: they are generally very important on the web and their pages usually get indexed very fast ('indexed' is a likely but not certain reading of the recording).
  <br><sub>`D2-C694` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Page quality is ultimately what decides whether a document is indexed, so focusing on quality is the most reliable way to get pages into Google's index.
  > "focusing on the quality is the most reliable way to get stuff in the index"
  <br><sub>`D2-C695` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extends [D1-C093](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection applies the negative signals that immediately block indexing: noindex (the likely reading of one unclear word), expired unavailable_after dates, soft 404s, non-canonical duplicates, spam signals and other policies.
  <br><sub>`D2-C696` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag), [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection drops a document carrying a noindex rule if it was not already dropped earlier in processing (noindex is a likely but not certain reading of the transcript, supported by the later mention of noindex among the Page indexing report reasons).
  <br><sub>`D2-C697` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en), [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Extends [D1-C106](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection checks for the robots unavailable_after rule and its date, and drops a page from the index once that date is reached.
  <br><sub>`D2-C698` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Extends [D2-C100](../day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-08`, the glossary term *unavailable_after*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Use the unavailable_after robots rule on pages with a known end date, such as event pages, time-limited offers or job ads, so that index selection drops them automatically when the date passes instead of leaving expired pages in search results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C699` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · [Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet, and X-Robots-Tag specifications](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag) · Used by `DEV-IDX-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C700` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/troubleshoot-crawling-errors) · Extends [D1-C073](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Extends [D2-C334](../day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google already has duplicate information for a document, for example when reprocessing it, index selection uses it to drop non-canonical duplicates from further processing, so that, as the speaker put it, only canonicals end up in search results (a simplification; see D2-C703).
  <br><sub>`D2-C701` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization), [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Extends [D1-C128](../day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) · Extends [D2-C345](../day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation says a search result usually points to the canonical page, but the other pages in a duplicate cluster are alternate versions that may be served in different contexts, for example a mobile page for a user on a mobile device.
  <br><sub>`D2-C702` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · is the documentation · [What is canonicalization](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization), [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** 'Only canonicals end up in search results' as said on stage is a simplification: non-canonical duplicates are dropped from the index, but Google's documentation says an alternate from the same cluster can still be shown in some contexts, such as a mobile version to a mobile user.
  <br><sub>`D2-C703` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection loads most of Google's spam signals and acts as a gatekeeper so that no spam enters search results.
  > "index selection acts as a gatekeeper, ensuring that no spam enters our search results"
  <br><sub>`D2-C704` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection also applies other policies, covering egregious violations and, in a less certain reading of the transcript, content Google is legally not allowed to index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C705` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Content policies for Google Search](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/10622781?hl=en)</sub>

- **[Stage]** 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
  > "The first one is kind of nastier."
  <br><sub>`D2-C706` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C097](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extends [D1-C065](../day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`, the glossary term *Discovered – currently not indexed*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Page indexing report help says a 'Discovered – currently not indexed' page was found but not crawled yet, typically because Google wanted to crawl it but expected the crawl to overload the site, so it rescheduled the crawl.
  <br><sub>`D2-C707` · Google Search Console Help · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · is the documentation · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`, the glossary term *Discovered – currently not indexed*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem.
  <br><sub>`D2-C708` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C098](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Site owners can influence 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by getting other URLs of the site indexed and showing Google's systems that the site's content is good and useful to users.
  <br><sub>`D2-C709` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C093](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Repeatedly submitting 'Discovered – currently not indexed' URLs does not change why they wait, because the status reflects a crawl-scheduling decision; raise the site's demonstrated quality instead, for example by improving or removing weak pages that are already indexed.
  <br><sub>`D2-C710` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index?</sub>

- **[Stage]** 'Crawled – currently not indexed' in Search Console is an index selection decision: Google crawled and processed the page but decided not to keep it in the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C711` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`, the glossary term *Crawled – currently not indexed*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Page indexing report help says a 'Crawled – currently not indexed' page was crawled but not indexed, may or may not be indexed in the future, and does not need to be resubmitted for crawling.
  <br><sub>`D2-C712` · Google Search Console Help · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · is the documentation · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`, the glossary term *Crawled – currently not indexed*</sub>

- **[Stage]** If content quality is even across a site, a page reported as 'Crawled – currently not indexed' may be using a different template that keeps Google from understanding where its content is.
  <br><sub>`D2-C713` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Used by `DEV-HTM-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most of the time a quality issue rather than a technical one: the pages are usually low quality or useless for the index, for example duplicates or soft 404s.
  > "most of the time it is actually a quality issue"
  <br><sub>`D2-C714` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C098](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The first thing to check for pages reported as 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is whether their quality is on par with the parts of the site that Google does index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C715` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat 'Crawled – currently not indexed' as a quality audit list: compare those URLs with indexed pages of the same type for thin, duplicate or soft-404-like content and for template differences before looking for technical faults.
  <br><sub>`D2-C716` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · Extends [D1-C098](../day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Search Console's Page indexing report is the place to check for index selection issues, and its not-indexed reasons are useful when testing changes on a site.
  <br><sub>`D2-C717` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Extends [D1-C368](../day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Not-indexed reasons in the Page indexing report include pages excluded by a noindex rule and 'Alternate page with proper canonical tag'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C718` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Page indexing report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>
